clue.text: Dry film director tours top cinema with Lawrence

indicators.note: to tour a place is to go all round it, so the director's name wraps around the next letter
the top of a word written across is its opening letter, so only the start is kept

blocks.note: Vittorio De Sica, the Italian director of Bicycle Thieves
first letter of cinema
T. E. Lawrence, Lawrence of Arabia

explanation.surface: A film director takes Lawrence on a tour of a leading cinema.
explanation.walkthrough: DE SICA goes round C, giving DESICCA, and T. E. Lawrence's initials follow: DESICCATE.
explanation.definitionFit: To desiccate something is to remove its moisture completely, so the verb is a straightforward synonym of dry.

clue.text: Oo, dear!

blocks.note: two noughts, and a nought in cricket is a duck, so two of them make the plural
a homely British term of endearment, as in 'Ta

explanation.walkthrough: 'Oo, dear!' reads as a mild exclamation of dismay; split it and the two letters O are zeros, while 'dear' is a form of address. In cricket a batsman out for nought has made a duck.
explanation.definitionFit: Two zero scores in cricket are a pair of ducks, and northern British speech calls a friend or loved one ducks.

clue.text: One of the crew pulls up to take note on board

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means the word is read from bottom to top
taking something aboard means holding it inside, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: to pull is to draw
te is the seventh note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: A crew member hauls up a musical note on a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: SWARD with TE placed inside gives S-TE-WARD. 'On board' finishes the nautical picture and doubles as the hint at a ship's crew.
explanation.definitionFit: A steward serves passengers on a ship or aircraft, so is a member of its crew.

clue.text: See 10
See 24
Ninety-one regions reformed, getting rid of spooks

indicators.note: regions that are reformed are reorganised, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: ninety in Roman numerals
one in Roman numerals
taken as written

explanation.surface: Ninety-one administrative regions are reorganised, and the ghosts are cleared out.
explanation.definitionFit: Exorcising is driving out evil spirits or ghosts, and spooks is informal for ghosts.

clue.text: Overfish in Essex?

definitions.note: the whole clue points to a place in Essex; the question mark flags the split word

blocks.note: on can mean over, as a lid is on or over a pot
the gar is a long-snouted fish

explanation.walkthrough: 'Overfish' looks like one verb; split it into Over and fish. ONGAR is a small market town in Essex, east of London.
explanation.definitionFit: Ongar, or Chipping Ongar, is a town in the county of Essex, so it is something located there.

clue.text: Hereafter ... or the next?

blocks.note: the life after death
as in 'this world and the next', the world beyond this one

explanation.walkthrough: Both halves name the spiritual realm beyond death, the second by the stock phrase 'this world and the next'.
explanation.definitionFit: The otherworld is the realm of the dead or the spirits, which is what the hereafter and the next world both mean.

clue.text: Silly person's rubbish

blocks.note: a British colloquialism for a fool
British slang for odds and ends, bits and pieces, junk

explanation.walkthrough: The possessive suggests a fool's junk; the 's is just 'is', joining two meanings of one British slang word.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang, gubbins means both a foolish person and miscellaneous junk or paraphernalia.

clue.text: Went off and again stood around, say

blocks.note: the prefix meaning again
to stand a round of drinks is to treat everyone; 'say' warns this is one example of treating

explanation.surface: Someone left, then hung about once more.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stood around' looks like loitering, but read it as 'stood a round' of drinks, which is treating people.
explanation.definitionFit: To retreat is to withdraw or move back, so went off in the sense of withdrew matches retreated.

clue.text: A conformist monk?

definitions.note: a cryptic reading: a being of the robe; the question mark admits the pun

blocks.note: first meaning: someone who always sticks to routine
second meaning: a monk wears a religious robe, so is literally a being of that garment

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase for a person of fixed routine is read literally: a habit is also the robe a monk wears.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who always follows the same routine is described by this idiom, which fits a conformist.

clue.text: Want self-contained central yard beside town?

indicators.note: the central part of a word is its middle, so its outer letters are discarded

blocks.note: s/c is the property-advert abbreviation for a self-contained flat
the two middle letters of yard
a large town is a city

explanation.surface: Someone wants a self-contained flat with a central courtyard near town, like an estate agent's listing.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads like a property wish-list; 'Want' is the definition, a noun meaning lack.
explanation.definitionFit: Want as a noun means a lack or shortage, which is what scarcity means.

clue.text: Old-timer's scoffing free curries, eating 50

definitions.note: an old-fashioned word for scoffing or jeering

indicators.note: set free, the letters are loosed from their order and rearranged
something eating another takes it inside, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: taken as written
L is fifty in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: An old man wolfs down fifty free curries.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scoffing' suggests gobbling food, which fits the curries, but here it means mocking; 'Old-timer's' marks the answer as archaic.
explanation.definitionFit: Scurrile is an archaic form of scurrilous, meaning coarsely jeering or abusive, so an old word for scoffing in the mocking sense.

clue.text: A bun in the oven, in the family way

definitions.text: A bun in the oven, in the family way

blocks.clueFragment: A bun in the oven, in the family way
blocks.note: surface reading: two slang phrases for being pregnant
setter's reading: a literal bun baking in a domestic oven, done the way families do it

explanation.walkthrough: Both phrases are idioms for pregnancy, but read literally they describe a bun cooking in a household kitchen.
explanation.definitionFit: Baking done in a domestic kitchen rather than a shop is this, so a bun in the family oven qualifies.

clue.text: Still eating up fungus? Be showing some consideration!

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading the word from bottom to top
eating something takes it inside, so one word goes within the other

blocks.note: still and calm
the cep is an edible mushroom, the porcino

explanation.surface: Someone is told to mind their manners while still eating up the mushrooms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Still eating up' looks like a single action at table; Still is the outer word, and up turns the mushroom round inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Being respectful means having regard for others' feelings, so it is showing some consideration.

clue.text: Spreads reveal Sir Alec dropping 50% with 100 sets of deliveries

indicators.note: dropping half the name means losing its second half and keeping only the front

blocks.note: Sir Alec Bedser, the England fast-medium bowler of the 1940s and 50s
C is a hundred in Roman numerals
in cricket an over is a set of six balls bowled

explanation.surface: A cricketing story: Sir Alec Bedser bowls a hundred overs.
explanation.walkthrough: Alec Bedser was a famous English bowler, which suits the cricket surface; half of BEDSER is BED.
explanation.definitionFit: Spreads are coverings laid over a bed, such as bedspreads, which are bedcovers.

clue.text: Perhaps Venetian's cannabis is what makes us undiscerning

blocks.note: a Venetian blind is one kind of window blind, hence 'perhaps'; the 's carries over
pot is slang for cannabis

explanation.surface: A drug-fuelled stupor from Venice dulls our judgment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Venetian' suggests a person from Venice, but it is the slatted window blind.
explanation.definitionFit: A blind spot is an area where a person lacks understanding or judgment, so it leaves us undiscerning.

clue.text: Where film actors start?

blocks.note: actors filming are working at the studio location, split as two words
a beginning

explanation.walkthrough: Read as two words it is where actors are during a shoot; as one word it means a beginning.
explanation.definitionFit: An onset is the beginning of something, especially something unpleasant like an illness, so it is a start.

clue.text: Awaken in order to exclaim "Buenos dias!"

indicators.note: the letters sit inside the phrase, in their original sequence, rather than shuffled

blocks.note: the letters run across the gap between the first two words

explanation.surface: Someone must wake up so they can greet the morning in Spanish.
explanation.definitionFit: To imbue is to inspire or instil feelings in someone, so in the sense of arousing an emotion it is to awaken.

clue.text: Italian port takes everything back for a plant

indicators.note: taking something back means turning it the other way, so the word is read in reverse

blocks.note: Bari is a port on Italy's Adriatic coast
everything is all

explanation.surface: An Italian port reclaims everything for a factory or industrial site.
explanation.definitionFit: Barilla is a saltwort plant once burnt to make soda ash, so it is a plant by definition.

clue.text: Peru deals in Scotch - is made to pay for it

indicators.note: to scotch a plan is to wreck it, so these words are broken up and remade

blocks.note: PE is Peru's international code
taken as written

explanation.surface: Peru trades in Scotch whisky and has to pay a price for it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scotch' reads as whisky, the goods being traded, but it is the verb meaning to wreck.
explanation.definitionFit: To be penalised is to be punished with a penalty, so it means being made to pay for a misdeed.

clue.text: Bush is provoked by Amis novel involving Ms Basinger

indicators.note: novel means new, so the name takes on a new arrangement
to involve something is to take it in, so one piece is placed inside

blocks.note: taken as written
Kim Basinger, the American actress

explanation.surface: A politician named Bush is riled by a Martin Amis novel featuring Kim Basinger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bush' looks like the US president; it is the definition, a shrub. 'Novel' looks like a book by Amis, but signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Skimmia is an evergreen shrub with red berries, often grown in gardens, so it is a bush.

clue.text: Long bridge-builder gets Twombly to sleep

blocks.note: Dorman Long was the Middlesbrough firm that built the Sydney Harbour Bridge
Cy Twombly, the American painter

explanation.surface: A long-serving bridge-builder hands the painter Twombly something to send him to sleep.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Long' looks like an adjective, but it is part of the company name Dorman Long, the British engineering firm that built Sydney Harbour Bridge.
explanation.definitionFit: Dormancy is a state of rest or inactivity, as with a hibernating animal, which is a kind of sleep.

clue.text: Leave to take out cash

blocks.note: to retire or depart
to get money out of a bank account

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as permission to go to the cashpoint; the two halves are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means both to depart or retreat from a place and to remove money from a bank account.

clue.text: Bellyache, wife having left ... get coupling!

indicators.note: the wife having left means her letter has gone from the word

blocks.note: to bellyache is to complain
W is the abbreviation for wife

explanation.surface: A man moans that his wife has walked out, and is urged to find a new partner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coupling' suggests pairing up romantically; it is a mechanical joint.
explanation.definitionFit: A hinge is a jointed device that joins a door or lid to its frame, so it is a coupling.

clue.text: See 21
Service an area of land and make a big killing

blocks.note: Mass is a church service
an acre is a measure of land area

explanation.surface: Selling a plot of land after a service lets someone make a big profit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make a big killing' looks like the idiom for profiting hugely, but here it is literal slaughter.
explanation.definitionFit: To massacre is to slaughter many people at once, so it means carrying out killing on a large scale.

clue.text: Transport cafe is supportin' the cigarette girl

blocks.note: a pull-in is a British roadside cafe for lorry drivers; the rest is read as part of a name
pulling for someone is cheering them on; Bizet's heroine works in a cigarette factory

explanation.walkthrough: Carmen, in Bizet's opera, works in a Seville cigarette factory. 'Pullin' for' is rooting for, with the dropped g mirrored by 'supportin''; a pull-in is a British transport cafe.
explanation.definitionFit: Pulling for someone means backing them, and a pull-in is a roadside diner, so the invented name for a lorry-drivers' cafe fits.

clue.text: Scots pair, nothing disheartened, acquire a burr

indicators.note: losing its heart means losing all its inner letters, leaving just the ends

blocks.note: twa is Scots for two
first and last letters of nothing

explanation.surface: A Scottish couple, losing heart over nothing, pick up a rolling accent.
explanation.definitionFit: A burr is a distinctive regional accent, as is a twang, though twang usually means a nasal one.

clue.text: Poor condition of large property in the Fens?

blocks.note: a humble or degraded state in life
the Fens are flat, low-lying marshland in eastern England, so an estate there sits low

explanation.walkthrough: The Fens are low-lying drained marshes in East Anglia, so a big landholding there is literally low-lying.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone in a low estate is in a humble, wretched situation, an old phrase for poor circumstances.
